Result & Option: `Result<T, E>` for recoverable errors. `Option<T>` for nullable values. `?` operator propagates errors. `unwrap()` and `expect()` extract values or panic. `ok_or()` converts Option to Result.
The ? Operator: `?` unwraps `Result` or `Option`, returning early on error/None. Converts error types via `From` trait. Only works in functions returning Result, Option, or types implementing `FromResidual`.
Panic & Unrecoverable Errors: `panic!()` unwinds the stack (or aborts with `panic = "abort"`). Use for unrecoverable states. `unwrap`, `expect`, `unreachable!()`, `todo!()`, `unimplemented!()` all panic on use.
Custom Error Types: Implement `std::error::Error` for custom errors. Requires `Display` + `Debug`. `source()` method for error chaining. `Box<dyn Error>` for type-erased error handling.
thiserror Crate: thiserror derives `std::error::Error` with minimal boilerplate. Supports `#[error("...")]` for Display, `#[source]` for error chaining, and `#[from]` for automatic From impls.
anyhow / eyre Crates: anyhow provides `Result<T, anyhow::Error>` for application-level error handling. `bail!()` and `ensure!()` macros. Context method `.context()`. eyre is a similar alternative with better error reports.
Error Chaining: Errors chain via `source()` or `.context()`. The `?` operator auto-converts via `From`. Libraries define specific error types; apps use anyhow/eyre. `Error::source` iterates the chain.
Result Combinators: `map`, `map_err`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `ok`, `err`, `transpose` — these combinators transform Results without explicit match.

What is Rust: Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, speed, and concurrency. It guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector through its ownership system and zero-cost abstractions.
Rust Syntax Basics: Rust uses `fn` for functions, `let` for variables, and macros with `!`. Semicolons end expressions, blocks use curly braces. `main` is the program entry point. Statements vs expressions distinction is key.
Variables & Mutability: Variables are immutable by default. Use `mut` to make them mutable. `const` for compile-time constants. Shadowing redeclares a variable with `let`, allowing type changes.
Scalar Types: Four scalar types: integers (i8-u128, i64, usize), floats (f32, f64), bool, char. Integer overflow wraps in release, panics in debug. Underscores improve readability: `1_000_000`.
rustup & Toolchains: rustup manages Rust toolchains. Switch between stable, beta, nightly. `rustup target add` for cross-compilation. `rustup component add` for tools. `rustup show` displays active toolchain.

# shell commands
$ rustup install nightly
$ rustup default stable
$ rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
$ rustup component add rust-src
Cargo Basics: Cargo is Rust's build system and package manager. `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`, `cargo check`, `cargo clean`. Cargo.toml defines metadata and dependencies.

# shell commands
$ cargo new my_project --bin
$ cd my_project
$ cargo add serde --features derive
$ cargo run --release
$ cargo check
rustfmt: rustfmt auto-formats code according to style guidelines. `cargo fmt` formats the whole project. `rustfmt --check` verifies formatting in CI. Configure with `rustfmt.toml`.

# shell commands
$ cargo fmt
$ rustfmt --check src/main.rs
# rustfmt.toml
max_width = 100
edition = "2021"
Clippy: Clippy is Rust's linter with 550+ rules. `cargo clippy` catches common mistakes, non-idiomatic code, and performance pitfalls. `#[allow(clippy::...)]` silences specific lints.

# shell commands
$ cargo clippy
$ cargo clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic
$ cargo clippy --fix
rust-analyzer: rust-analyzer provides IDE support: code completion, goto-definition, type hints, inlay hints, rename, diagnostics. LSP server used by VS Code, Neovim, Emacs, and Zed.

if / else if / else: Conditions must be `bool` — no truthy/falsy coercion. `if` is an expression, assignable with `let`. All arms must return the same type. Blocks evaluate to their last expression.
Loops (loop, while, for): `loop` repeats forever until `break`. `while` loops on a condition. `for` iterates over iterators. `for (0..n)` is range syntax. Use `continue` to skip to next iteration.
Pattern Matching (match): `match` is Rust's powerful pattern matching. Arms must be exhaustive. Patterns can bind, match ranges (`..=`), use `|` for alternatives, and guards with `if`.
if let: `if let` combines `match` for a single pattern, ignoring others. Useful with `Option`, `Result`, and enums. Reduces boilerplate when only one arm matters.
while let: `while let` repeatedly matches a pattern until it fails. Common with iterators, `Option`-producing functions, and mutable borrow patterns.
Labeled Break & Continue: Loop labels (`'label`) disambiguate nested loops. `break 'label` exits the named loop. `continue 'label` skips to the next iteration of the named loop.
Loop Returning Values: `loop` can return a value with `break value`. `break` with no value returns `()`. Useful for retry logic or initializing values from fallible operations.

Ownership Rules: Each value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. Ownership can be moved. This guarantees memory safety without GC.
Move Semantics: Assigning or passing a value moves ownership unless the type implements `Copy`. Stack-only types (integers, bools, floats, chars, tuples of Copy types) are copied.
Borrowing & References: References borrow values without taking ownership. `&T` (immutable, shared). `&mut T` (mutable, exclusive). References must never outlive their referent.
Borrow Rules Deep: At any time: either one mutable reference, or any number of immutable references. References must always be valid. The borrow checker enforces this at compile time.
Split Borrows: Rust allows borrowing different fields of a struct simultaneously. The borrow checker tracks borrows at the field level, enabling mutable access to disjoint fields.
Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL): NLL makes the borrow checker smarter: borrows end when they're last used, not at the end of the scope. This reduces friction with the borrow checker significantly.
Slices: Slices are dynamically-sized views into contiguous sequences. `&str` is a string slice. `&[T]` is an array slice. They are fat pointers (ptr + length) and never own data.
Interior Mutability: Interior mutability allows mutating data through shared references. Provided by `Cell<T>` (Copy types, no threads), `RefCell<T>` (runtime borrow checking, no threads), and `Mutex<T>` (thread-safe).
RefCell & Borrow Checking at Runtime: RefCell enforces borrow rules at runtime — panics on violation. `borrow()` returns `Ref<T>`, `borrow_mut()` returns `RefMut<T>`. Useful when the compiler can't verify correctness.

Function Declaration: Functions use `fn` with snake_case naming. Parameters require type annotations. Return type is `-> Type`. The last expression in a block is implicitly returned. Early return with `return`.
Methods & Associated Functions: Methods are functions defined in `impl` blocks with a `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` parameter. Associated functions (like constructors) don't take `self` and are called with `::`.
Closures: Closures are anonymous functions that capture their environment. `||` syntax. Traits: `Fn` (immutable capture), `FnMut` (mutable capture), `FnOnce` (consume capture). Each closure has a unique type.
Diverging Functions & Never Type: `!` (never type) indicates a function that never returns. `panic!()`, `loop {}`, `todo!()`, `unreachable!()` all diverge. Used in match arms that must match any type.
Function Pointers: `fn(T) -> U` is a function pointer type, not a closure. Cannot capture environment. Useful for callbacks and FFI. Coerces from closures that don't capture.
Where Clauses: `where` clauses specify trait bounds after the function signature. More readable for complex generics. Same semantics as inline bounds. Required for some complex bound patterns.
Higher-Order Functions: Functions can take closures as parameters using generic bounds. Iterator adapters like `map`, `filter`, `fold` enable functional pipelines. Combinators compose nicely.

Tuples: Tuples group values of different types. Fixed length. Destructure with pattern matching or index syntax `.0`, `.1`. Unit tuple `()` is the empty tuple, representing absence of value.
Arrays: Arrays have fixed length `[T; N]`. Stored on stack. Bounds-checked at runtime. Slices `&[T]` borrow array elements. `[0; 100]` creates an array filled with the same value.
Vectors: `Vec<T>` is a growable heap-allocated array. Use `vec![]` macro. Amortized O(1) push. `Vec::with_capacity(n)` pre-allocates. `drain`, `retain`, `splice` are powerful methods.
Strings (&str vs String): `&str` is a borrowed string slice (UTF-8). `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer. `&str` to `String` via `.to_string()` or `String::from()`. Strings are not `Index` due to UTF-8.
Structs: Structs define custom data with named fields. Use `impl` blocks for methods. Field init shorthand when variable matches field name. Struct update syntax `..other` fills remaining fields.
Tuple Structs: Tuple structs have unnamed fields accessed by position. Newtype pattern wraps a single type. Good for type safety without field name overhead. `struct Wrapper(T)`.
Unit Structs: Unit structs have no fields — act as markers or flags. Zero size. Useful for implementing traits without data, or as phantom types with `PhantomData`.
Enums: Enums define sum types with variants. Variants can hold data (tuple or struct). `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` are the most common enums. `match` enforces exhaustive handling.

Generics: Generics abstract over types, enabling code reuse. Monomorphization generates specialized code per concrete type at compile time. Type parameters are declared with `<T>`.
Traits: Traits define shared behavior (like interfaces). Types implement traits with `impl Trait for Type`. Traits can provide default method implementations. Must be in scope to use methods.
Derive Macros: `#[derive(...)]` auto-implements common traits: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default, PartialOrd, Ord. Saves boilerplate and ensures correctness.
Supertraits: Supertraits express that one trait extends another. `trait A: B` means types implementing A must also implement B. Used with `where Self: SuperTrait` for method access.
Trait Objects & dyn Trait: Trait objects enable dynamic dispatch via vtable. `dyn Trait` is unsized — must be behind a pointer (`&dyn Trait`, `Box<dyn Trait>`). Objects must be object-safe (no generic methods, no Self by value).
impl Trait Syntax: `impl Trait` in argument position is like a generic. In return position, it returns an opaque type implementing Trait. Cannot return multiple types. Useful for returning closures/iterators.
Associated Types: Associated types define placeholder types within a trait. One implementation per type — unlike generics which allow multiple impls. Used extensively in Iterator, Deref, and operator traits.
Blanket Implementations: Blanket impls implement a trait for all types satisfying bounds. `impl<T: Display> ToString for T {}` is a blanket impl. They allow adding methods to all types meeting criteria.
Trait Bounds & where Clauses: Trait bounds constrain generics. Multiple bounds: `T: Clone + Debug`. `where` clauses improve readability. `impl Trait` as shorthand. `?Sized` opts out of the implicit Sized bound.

Vec: `Vec<T>` is the primary sequence type — growable, heap-allocated, contiguous. Amortized O(1) push/pop. O(n) insert/remove. `with_capacity` pre-allocates. `drain`, `splice`, `retain` for advanced operations.
VecDeque: `VecDeque<T>` is a double-ended queue with O(1) push/pop at both ends. Ring buffer internally. Use for queue/sliding window patterns. `make_contiguous()` for slice access.
HashMap & HashSet: `HashMap<K, V>` stores key-value pairs with O(1) average lookup. `HashSet<T>` is a set of unique values. Both require keys to implement `Hash + Eq`. `entry()` API handles insert-or-update.
BTreeMap & BTreeSet: `BTreeMap` / `BTreeSet` maintain sorted order with O(log n) operations. Keys must implement `Ord`. Use when order matters or for range queries. `range()` returns entries within bounds.
BinaryHeap: `BinaryHeap<T>` is a max-heap priority queue. O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop. Use `Reverse<T>` for min-heap. `into_sorted_vec()` drains in order.
LinkedList: `LinkedList<T>` is a doubly-linked list. O(1) push/pop at both ends. Split/append operations. Generally slower than Vec/VecDeque due to cache behavior. Use for heavy splitting.

Box<T> (Heap Allocation): `Box<T>` allocates on the heap. Used for recursive types (linked lists), trait objects (`Box<dyn Trait>`), and large data moved infrequently. Derefs to `&T` / `&mut T`.
Rc<T> (Reference Counting): `Rc<T>` enables shared ownership within a single thread. `Rc::clone()` increments reference count. `strong_count` / `weak_count`. `Weak<T>` prevents cycles. Use `Arc` for threads.
Arc<T> (Atomic RC): `Arc<T>` is `Rc` + atomic reference counting — thread-safe. `Arc::clone()` is atomic. Pair with `Mutex<T>` for mutable shared state. `Arc<[T]>` for shared slices.
Cell<T> & RefCell<T>: `Cell<T>` provides interior mutability for Copy types (no borrow checking — just copy in/out). `RefCell<T>` provides interior mutability for any type, checking borrows at runtime.
Cow (Clone-on-Write): `Cow<'a, B>` abstracts borrowed vs owned data. `Cow::Borrowed(&str)` / `Cow::Owned(String)`. Call `.to_mut()` to get mutable access, cloning if borrowed. Ideal for read-mostly APIs.
Pin<T>: `Pin<T>` ensures a value is never moved again. Required for self-referential structs and async generators. `Pin<&mut T>` / `Pin<Box<T>>`. Unsafe to construct. Foundation of async Rust.
Drop Order: Variables drop in reverse declaration order. Struct fields drop in declaration order. `std::mem::forget` skips Drop. `ManuallyDrop` controls Drop. Nested values: outer drops first, then inner.
Mutex, RwLock, Condvar: `Mutex<T>` guards shared data across threads. `RwLock<T>` allows concurrent reads / exclusive writes. `Condvar` blocks threads until a condition is met. `PoisonError` on panic.
Channels (mpsc): `std::sync::mpsc` provides multi-producer, single-consumer channels. `Sender` clones for multiple producers. `Receiver` has `recv`, `try_recv`, `iter`. `crossbeam` offers multi-consumer variants.
Pinning & Pin<P>:
Pin

ensures a value won't be moved in memory. Essential for self-referential structs (e.g., async Futures). `Pin>` (heap-pinned), `Pin<&mut T>` (stack-pinned via `pin!` macro). Once pinned, cannot safely move. `Unpin` auto-trait: most types are Unpin (move OK). Async blocks/futures are `!Unpin` (not Unpin). Unsafe `get_unchecked_mut` to mutate pinned data. PhantomPinned marker make a type !Unpin.

Modules & Paths: `mod` declares a module. Files and directories mirror modules. `pub` controls visibility. `super` / `crate` / `self` keywords for paths. `pub(crate)` restricts to crate.
Re-exports: `pub use` re-exports items at a different path, making them part of the public API. Useful for flattening module hierarchies and renaming. `pub(crate) use` for internal re-exports.
Nested Modules & File System: Modules can be nested inline or in files. `mod foo;` looks for `foo.rs` or `foo/mod.rs`. `mod foo { ... }` for inline. The 2018 edition uses the `foo.rs` convention.
Cargo.toml & Crate Types: Crate types: `bin` (binary), `lib` (library), `cdylib` (C-compatible dynamic lib), `staticlib`, `proc-macro`. `edition` field selects Rust edition. `[profile.*]` for optimization settings.

[package]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
[lib]
crate-type = ["lib", "cdylib"]
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = true
Dependencies & Features: Dependencies from crates.io, git, or path. `features` enable conditional compilation. `default-features = false` to opt out. `[target.'cfg(...)'.dependencies]` for platform-specific deps.
Workspaces: Workspaces manage multiple crates in one project. Shared `target/` and `Cargo.lock`. Members listed in `[workspace]`. `cargo build -p specific-crate` to build a single member.
Conditional Compilation: `#[cfg()]` gates code on target, feature, or OS. `cfg!()` is a runtime boolean. `#[cfg_attr(...)]` conditionally applies attributes. `cfg(test)` gates test-only code.

Basic Lifetime Annotations: Lifetimes (`'a`) annotate how long references are valid. Prevent dangling references. The borrow checker validates lifetimes at compile time. Elision rules handle common patterns automatically.
Lifetime Elision Rules: Three elision rules: 1) each input reference gets its own lifetime. 2) with one input lifetime, output gets that lifetime. 3) with `&self`/`&mut self`, output gets self's lifetime. These cover 95%+ of cases.
'static Lifetime: `'static` references live for the entire program. String literals have type `&'static str`. `Box::leak` produces `&'static mut`. Const items are effectively static.
Lifetime Bounds & Subtyping: `'a: 'b` means 'a outlives 'b (is a subtype of 'b). Required when one lifetime must strictly outlive another. Common in structs and complex function signatures.
Higher-Ranked Trait Bounds (HRTB): HRTBs with `for<'a>` express that a bound must hold for all lifetimes. `Fn(&i32)` is sugar for `for<'a> Fn(&'a i32)`. Required for trait objects and closure bounds.
Variance: Variance describes how lifetimes compose: `&'a T` is covariant in 'a, `&'a mut T` is invariant in 'a, `fn(T) -> U` is contravariant in T. `Cell<T>` makes T invariant. Important for type safety.
Lifetime Coercion: Rust coerces shorter lifetimes to longer ones when safe. `&'a T` coerces to `&'b T` if `'a: 'b`. String `&str` to `&str` with shorter lifetime. Occurs implicitly at coercion sites.
NLL Deep: NLL (Non-Lexical Lifetimes) allows borrows to end before the scope ends. Two-phase borrows let reborrowing during method calls. The borrow checker uses a location-aware analysis.

async/await Basics: `async fn` returns a `Future`. `.await` polls the future to completion. Futures are lazy — they do nothing until awaited or polled. An executor is required to drive futures.
Tokio Runtime Deep: Tokio provides a multi-threaded (work-stealing) or single-threaded runtime. `#[tokio::main]` attribute sets up the runtime. Key components: reactor (I/O events), scheduler (tasks), timers.
Async Traits: Async traits require nightly or workarounds. `async-trait` crate desugars to `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`. Upcoming native async traits in Rust will remove this overhead.
select! & join! Macros: `tokio::select!` waits on multiple futures, completing when the first finishes. `futures::join!` awaits multiple futures concurrently. `try_join!` returns on first error.
join_all / FuturesUnordered: `futures::future::join_all` awaits a collection of futures, returning all results. `FuturesUnordered` polls a set of futures, yielding results as they complete — ideal for dynamic workloads.
Async Streams: `Stream` trait is the async version of `Iterator`. `StreamExt` provides `next()`, `map`, `filter`, `fold`. `tokio_stream` and `futures` libraries. `async-stream` macro creates streams.
Pin Projection: Pin projection allows safely accessing fields of a pinned struct using `pin_project` or `pin_utils`. Critical for self-referential async state machines. `#[pin_project]` attribute handles the unsafe parts.
Async Sync Primitives: Tokio provides async-aware synchronisation: `Mutex` (hold across .await), `RwLock`, `Semaphore`, `Barrier`, `Notify`, `watch`, `broadcast` channels. Never hold a std::sync::Mutex across .await.

Raw Pointers: `*const T` and `*mut T` are raw pointers with no safety guarantees. Can be null, dangling, or aliased. Dereferencing requires `unsafe`. Create from references with `as *const T`. Used for FFI and perf.
Unsafe Functions & Blocks: `unsafe fn` marks an unsafe function that callers must wrap in `unsafe {}`. `unsafe` blocks opt into: deref raw pointers, call unsafe fns, access mutable statics, implement unsafe traits.
Calling C (FFI): `extern "C"` declares functions from C libraries. `#[link(name = "...")]` links native libs. `#[no_mangle]` prevents name mangling. `unsafe` to call. `libc` crate provides C type aliases.
#[repr(C)] & repr Attributes: `#[repr(C)]` lays out struct fields like C (no reordering). `#[repr(transparent)]` wraps a single field with same layout. `#[repr(packed)]` removes padding. `#[repr(align(n))]` sets alignment.
no_std & Global Allocator: `#![no_std]` removes the standard library for embedded/kernel targets. Use `core` and `alloc` crates. `#[global_allocator]` replaces the default allocator. `alloc_error_handler` for OOM.
#[link] & extern Blocks: `#[link(name = "foo", kind = "static")]` links native libraries. `extern "C"` (or "system", "stdcall") blocks declare foreign functions. `#[link_name = "actual_name"]` overrides the symbol name.
Exposing Rust to C (cdylib): `#[no_mangle]` with `extern "C"` exposes Rust functions to C. `CString` creates null-terminated strings. `Cargo.toml` needs `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]`. FFI-safe types only.

Builder Pattern: Builder pattern constructs complex objects with many optional parameters. Methods return `&mut Self` or `Self` for chaining. `build()` consumes the builder and produces the final value.
RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initializa: RAII ties resource lifetime to scope. Files, locks, and memory are released in `Drop`. `MutexGuard`, `File`, `Box` all use RAII. Cannot forget to release — the compiler handles it.
Newtype Pattern: Wrap a single type in a tuple struct for type safety and trait impls. Zero-cost abstraction — the wrapper is optimized away. Used for units, IDs, and implementing external traits on external types.
Deref Pattern & Deref Coercion: Implementing `Deref<Target=U>` allows smart pointers to behave like references. `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, `Arc<T>` all deref to their inner type. `DerefMut` for mutable deref. Chains `.` auto-derefs.
Drop Order in Composed Types: Struct fields drop in declaration order. Tuple fields drop in index order. Slices/vectors drop elements front-to-back. Closures drop their captures when the closure drops.
Typestate Pattern: Typestate encoding uses the type system to enforce state transitions. Methods consume the current state and return the next. Invalid transitions are compile-time errors. Common in builders and protocols.
Interior Mutability Patterns: Interior mutability: mutate data through shared references. Types: Cell<T> (Copy types, no sync), RefCell<T> (non-Copy, runtime borrow checking, no sync), OnceCell<T> (write once, no sync). Sync versions: Mutex<T>, RwLock<T>, AtomicBool/isize/ptr, OnceLock<T>. RefCell borrows checked at runtime — panics on double borrow. Rc<RefCell<T>> for shared mutable ownership (single-thread). Arc<Mutex<T>> for multi-thread.

Unit Tests: Unit tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file. Test functions are annotated with `#[test]`. Assert with `assert!`, `assert_eq!`, `assert_ne!`. `#[should_panic]` for expected panics.
Integration Tests: Integration tests live in `tests/` directory at crate root. Each file is a separate crate. They test the public API only. `cargo test --test integration_test_name` runs a specific file.
Doc Tests: Doc tests are code blocks in `///` or `//!` docs. Run with `cargo test`. Code blocks with ` ``` ` are compiled and run. ` ```ignore ` skips compilation. ` ```no_run ` compiles but doesn't run.
Test Organization & Attributes: `#[cfg(test)]` only compiles test modules. `#[test]` marks a test. `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]`. `#[ignore]` skips a test. `#[bench]` for benchmarks (nightly). `cargo test -- --nocapture` for stdout.
Benchmarks: `cargo bench` runs benchmark functions with `#[bench]` (nightly). Or use the `criterion` crate (stable). Criterion measures time, generates reports, and detects performance regressions.
Property Testing with proptest: proptest generates many random inputs to verify properties. `proptest!` macro defines strategies. `#[proptest]` is an alternative. Checks invariants hold for all inputs. Finds edge cases.
Mocking & Test Doubles: Mock objects simulate dependencies. `mockall` crate generates mock types from trait definitions. `#[automock]` for single methods. Use with dependency injection for isolated tests.

Declarative Macros (macro_rules!): `macro_rules!` matches patterns and generates code. Metavariables: `$expr`, `$ty`, `$ident`, `$stmt`, `$pat`, `$tt`. Repetition with `$()*`, `$()+`, `$()?`. Hygiene prevents name collisions.
Macro Patterns & Designators: Designators: `block`, `expr`, `ident`, `item`, `lifetime`, `literal`, `meta`, `pat`, `path`, `stmt`, `tt`, `ty`, `vis`. `tt` (token tree) is the most flexible — matches any single token group.
Procedural Macros (proc-macro): Procedural macros operate on the token stream. Three kinds: `#[derive]`, attribute-like `#[...]`, function-like `name!()`. Defined in proc-macro crates. `proc_macro::TokenStream` as input/output.
Derive Macros: Derive macros automatically implement traits. Custom derive macros use `#[proc_macro_derive(Name)]`. Generate impl blocks. The `syn` crate parses token streams. `quote` crate generates output tokens.
Attribute Macros: Attribute macros customize items they annotate. `#[proc_macro_attribute]` receives the attribute arguments and the annotated item tokens. Used for `#[tokio::main]`, `#[async_trait]`, etc.
Debugging Macros: `cargo expand` (cargo-expand) shows macro expansion output. `log_syntax!()` prints tokens during expansion. `trace_macros!()` logs all macro invocations. `stringify!()` converts to string.
Declarative Macro Patterns: Advanced macro_rules! patterns: TT muncher (recursive token tree processing), internal rules, hygiene control, token types (ident, expr, ty, pat, stmt, block, literal, tt, meta, lifetime, vis). Common: vec! (repeated expr), hashmap! (key=>value pairs), builder patterns. Repetition: `$($x:expr),*` (zero+), `$($x:expr),+` (one+). Use `@` for internal rules. Export with `#[macro_export]`.
